questions.questionText: What does ergonomics help determine in the industrial workplace?

options.text: How to discipline unsafe workers
How employees can work more effectively and safely based on body mechanics and workplace design
How to eliminate all manual work from production
How to increase production speed without changing workstations

questions.questionText: Which body areas are commonly affected by ergonomic problems?

options.text: Hand and wrist only
Shoulder and arm only
Back and neck only
All of the above — hands, wrists, shoulders, arms, back, and neck

questions.questionText: What is one benefit of keeping tools and materials directly in front of the body?

options.text: It increases the amount of twisting required
It encourages neutral movements and reduces awkward reaching
It makes lifting unnecessary
It eliminates all repetitive motion

questions.questionText: Which movement should be minimized to protect the lower back?

options.text: Turning with the feet
Twisting at the waist
Keeping the load close to the body
Bending at the knees

questions.questionText: What should employees do before lifting a load?

options.text: Lift quickly to test the weight
Size up the load and decide whether help or mechanical assistance is needed
Twist at the waist to build momentum
Hold the load away from the body for balance

questions.questionText: Employees should always try to lift heavy or awkward loads alone before asking for help.

options.text: True
False

questions.questionText: What can help reduce the physical stress of repetitive work?

options.text: Task rotation only
Mini-breaks only
Stretching only
All of the above — task rotation, mini-breaks, and stretching

questions.questionText: Why should power tools be kept clean and in good working condition?

options.text: So they are easier and safer to use
So employees can apply more force
So vibration exposure does not need to be controlled
So formal training is unnecessary

questions.questionText: What is a good seated posture practice for employees doing prolonged desk or assembly work?

options.text: Let the feet dangle freely below the chair
Sit without back support to strengthen core muscles
Support the lumbar region and keep feet flat on the floor or on a footrest
Lean forward for extended periods to stay alert

questions.questionText: What should employees do if they feel early signs of discomfort, numbness, tingling, or persistent pain?

options.text: Ignore it unless it becomes severe enough to affect work
Report it according to company procedure before it worsens
Work faster to finish the task before the discomfort increases
Stop using all tools permanently until evaluated

questions.questionText: What should be used when a load is too heavy for safe manual handling?

options.text: More speed to reduce total strain time
Mechanical assistance such as a cart, dolly, or hoist, or additional help
A twisting motion to generate lifting force
One-handed lifting to keep the other hand free

questions.questionText: A workstation may need to be adjusted because employees have different body sizes, reaches, and physical needs.

options.text: True
False

questions.questionText: What is the safest wrist position during tool use and repetitive assembly work?

options.text: Wrist bent downward (flexion)
Wrist bent upward and back (extension)
Wrist straight and neutral, similar to a handshake position
Wrist rotated fully with the palm facing down

questions.questionText: An employee can safely turn their upper body while their feet stay stationary when carrying a load.

options.text: True
False

questions.questionText: What is the primary purpose of taking brief mini-breaks during repetitive industrial work?

options.text: To comply with a mandatory OSHA 1910.900 break schedule
To allow employees time to check personal devices during the shift
To allow muscles to recover and reduce the buildup of repetitive strain
To reset the production cycle counter

lessons.ergonomics-overview:
**Understanding Ergonomics and How the Body Works**

Ergonomics is the process of fitting the job, tools, and work environment to the worker so tasks can be performed safely and efficiently. A well-designed job allows employees to work in neutral, natural positions. A poorly designed job may require repeated bending, twisting, overreaching, gripping, or awkward postures that force muscles and joints to work harder than they should. Key ergonomic risk factors include repetitive motion without adequate rest, awkward or extreme body positions, excessive force, heavy loads, vibration, poor workstation height, and prolonged sitting or standing. Ergonomic injuries often develop gradually — they may begin as minor discomfort, tightness, or fatigue. Workstations must be evaluated individually because employees have different body sizes, reaches, and physical needs. Early recognition and reporting are essential.
lessons.hand-wrist-ergonomics:
**Hand and Wrist Ergonomics**

The neutral wrist position — straight, similar to a handshake — places the least stress on the wrist. Employees should minimize wrist flexion (bending down), extension (bending up), and side-to-side deviation. Repetitive forceful gripping, prolonged trigger use, and vibration exposure all contribute to hand and wrist fatigue and can irritate nerves over time. Tools should be evaluated for weight, balance, handle shape, trigger tension, and vibration. Poorly balanced tools, handles with sharp edges, and tools with high trigger spring tension all increase fatigue and injury risk. Tools must be kept clean and in good working condition so they are easier and safer to use. Anti-vibration gloves or sleeves may help reduce vibration exposure when appropriate.
lessons.arm-shoulder-ergonomics:
**Arm and Shoulder Ergonomics**

The preferred neutral position keeps the upper arms near the sides and the forearms positioned comfortably near a 90-degree angle. Stressful shoulder and arm postures include raising the arms forward for long periods, reaching backward, working with arms extended away from the body, reaching across the body, and repeating the same arm movement without rest. Keeping frequently used tools and materials directly in front of the worker — rather than to the side or behind — reduces reaching, twisting, and awkward arm positions and encourages neutral movements. Workstation height is critical: the surface should be adjusted so arms do not need to be elevated or drooped. Employers should evaluate any tasks that require repeated overhead reaching or excessive force on the arms and shoulders.
lessons.back-neck-ergonomics:
**Back and Neck Ergonomics**

The back and neck are especially vulnerable to ergonomic injury. Movements to minimize include neck flexion and extension, side-to-side neck strain, twisting the lower back, bending at the waist, stooping, and working at surfaces that are too high or too low. For seated work, the lower back should be supported with lumbar support. Feet should rest flat on the floor or a footrest. For standing work, tools and materials should be within easy reach and work surfaces should support neutral arm and back positioning. Anti-fatigue mats, cushioned insoles, and footrests can help reduce leg and back fatigue during prolonged standing. When turning while carrying a load, always turn with the feet — never twist the upper body while the feet remain stationary.
lessons.safe-lifting:
**Safe Lifting and Material Handling**

Before every lift, size up the load: assess the weight, shape, size, grip, path of travel, and whether help or mechanical assistance is needed. Safe lifting steps: get close to the load, place feet securely, bend at the knees (not the waist), get a firm grip, keep the back straight, lift slowly with the legs, keep the load close to the body, and turn with the feet — never twist at the waist while carrying. Lower the load by reversing the process. If the load is heavy, bulky, unstable, or awkward, do not attempt it alone — get help or use a cart, dolly, pallet jack, hoist, or other approved mechanical assistance. For team lifts, lift in unison and communicate clearly before and during the move. Lifting safely is about controlling the load and protecting the body, not proving strength.
lessons.task-rotation-reporting:
**Task Rotation, Stretching, and Early Reporting**

Employees can reduce ergonomic strain by alternating between tasks, taking brief mini-breaks to allow muscles to recover, and performing gentle stretching during rest periods. Mini-breaks reduce the buildup of continuous strain from repetitive movements and loosen tight muscles before fatigue becomes injury. Stretching should be gentle and appropriate for the task — employees should follow company-approved guidance and avoid forcing movements that cause pain. Tools and equipment must be kept in good working condition because worn or damaged tools require extra force and generate more vibration. Most importantly, employees should report pain, discomfort, numbness, tingling, or fatigue early — before the problem worsens. Early reporting gives the workplace a chance to evaluate the task, adjust the workstation, and implement controls before a minor ache becomes a serious injury.

1.questionText: Industrial ergonomics is best described as:

options.text: A process for disciplining employees who adopt unsafe postures
Fitting the job, tools, and environment to the worker to reduce physical stress and prevent injury
Eliminating all manual tasks from industrial production
Increasing production speed through workstation redesign only

2.questionText: Musculoskeletal disorders caused by ergonomic hazards can affect which of the following?

options.text: Only the hands and wrists
Only the back and shoulders
Only the neck and arms
The hands, wrists, arms, shoulders, back, and neck

3.questionText: An employee keeps all frequently used parts directly in front of them at workstation height. The main ergonomic benefit is:

options.text: It requires the employee to stretch more often during the shift
It reduces awkward reaching and promotes neutral body positioning
It eliminates the need for tool maintenance and inspection
It increases production speed without changing posture

4.questionText: Which body movement puts the greatest strain on the lower back when combined with carrying a load?

options.text: Bending at the knees to lower the body
Keeping the load close to the body
Twisting at the waist
Turning with the feet in the direction of travel

5.questionText: Before picking up an unfamiliar or heavy load, an employee should:

options.text: Lift it quickly to determine the weight before deciding on technique
Assess the weight, size, grip, and travel path and decide whether help or equipment is needed
Twist to position the body before the lift for better leverage
Hold the load away from the body to test its balance

6.questionText: When a load is too heavy or awkward for one person, the correct response is to attempt the lift alone first and ask for help only if necessary.

options.text: True
False

7.questionText: Which combination of practices is most effective at reducing musculoskeletal strain from repetitive industrial tasks?

options.text: Increasing task speed to reduce total time on the repetitive task
Rotating between tasks, taking brief breaks, and stretching during rest periods
Wearing gloves for all repetitive work regardless of task type
Using only the non-dominant hand to preserve the dominant one

8.questionText: A power tool that vibrates excessively or has a worn or damaged grip should be:

options.text: Used with extra gripping force to maintain control
Reported and removed from service until repaired or replaced
Wrapped with tape to temporarily reduce vibration
Used only for short tasks until a replacement becomes available

9.questionText: For employees who perform seated work for extended periods, which practice best supports spinal health?

options.text: Sitting forward on the edge of the seat without back contact
Allowing feet to dangle to reduce lower body fatigue
Supporting the lower back and keeping feet flat on the floor or a footrest
Leaning back fully with arms raised above the head

10.questionText: An employee notices numbness in their hand during a repetitive assembly task. The appropriate response is:

options.text: Continue working to see if the feeling passes before end of shift
Report the symptom immediately so the task can be evaluated before the problem worsens
Work faster to finish before the numbness spreads
Stop using all tools until a medical provider clears the return to work

11.questionText: A shipping employee needs to move a pallet of materials that is too heavy to lift manually. What is the correct approach?

options.text: Use extra speed and momentum to complete the lift
Twist at the waist to generate additional force for the lift
Use a pallet jack, dolly, or ask for a team lift
Carry the load in multiple trips by hand regardless of total weight

12.questionText: A single workstation setup can safely accommodate all employees regardless of their individual height, reach, and body proportions.

options.text: True
False

13.questionText: Which of the following describes the recommended neutral wrist position for tool use and assembly work?

options.text: Wrist bent downward toward the floor (flexion)
Wrist bent upward and back (extension)
Wrist straight and in line with the forearm, similar to a handshake
Wrist rotated fully with the palm facing upward (supination)

14.questionText: Turning the upper body while keeping the feet stationary is an acceptable technique when carrying a load.

options.text: True
False

15.questionText: What is the primary ergonomic purpose of taking brief mini-breaks during repetitive industrial work?

options.text: To comply with a mandatory OSHA 1910.900 scheduled break requirement
To allow employees time for personal activities during the shift
To allow muscles to recover and reduce the buildup of repetitive strain
To reset the facility production cycle counter
